name: Squalene

lead: Squalene is a natural oil that the body makes and that appears in skin sebum. In skincare it is used as a light emollient, sourced from shark liver, olive or amaranth oil, or made synthetically.
Its appearance benefits are described mostly in terms of its skin-like origin; no published human trial was found testing it for acne, ageing or texture.

paras: It is an emollient that sits on and blends with the skin's lipid layer. In the body it is a step in making cholesterol.
Reviews summarised by Wikipedia report low toxicity and little allergy at cosmetic levels. Its many double bonds mean it can oxidise. Shark sourcing has been a conservation concern.

lead: Squalene is an oily hydrocarbon (C30H50) and an intermediate in the biosynthesis of sterols such as cholesterol. It takes its name from Squalus, the shark genus whose liver oil was its first major source, and it is also made by the human body and secreted in skin sebum.[1][2]

In personal care it is used as an emollient and lubricant in topical products. Sources include shark liver oil, olive oil and amaranth oil, plus synthetic and microbial production. Squalene is also an ingredient of oil-in-water emulsion adjuvants used in some vaccines.[1]

Toxicology reviews summarised by Wikipedia indicate low acute toxicity and little contact allergy at cosmetic concentrations.[1] The wiki found no published human trial testing squalene for an appearance outcome such as acne, wrinkles or skin texture.

paras: Squalene is a colourless to yellowish oil made of six isoprene units. Most plants, fungi and animals make it by joining two molecules of farnesyl pyrophosphate in a reaction catalysed by squalene synthase; it is then converted onward to sterols including cholesterol.[1][2]

The Japanese researcher Mitsumaru Tsujimoto reported an unsaponifiable fraction in deep-sea shark liver oil in 1906 and established the formula C30H50 in 1916. Paul Karrer and A. Helfenstein synthesised it in 1931.[1]

Deep-water shark liver oil is the richest natural source. Amaranth oil (about 1 to 7 percent) and olive oil (about 0.2 to 0.5 percent) are plant sources, and synthetic and engineered-microbe routes exist.[1] In 2020 conservation groups raised concern that vaccine demand for squalene could affect shark populations.[1]

Squalene is a component of human sebum, and the skin-identical origin is the usual rationale for its use as a lightweight emollient in moisturisers and oils.[1][2] Grokipedia describes it as compatible with skin lipids and as an antioxidant-like ingredient because of its many double bonds, though it also notes that it can react with oxidants.[2]

Toxicology studies summarised on Wikipedia indicate low acute toxicity and little irritation or contact allergy at cosmetic concentrations.[1] Oxidised squalene (squalene peroxide) is discussed in the dermatology literature as a component of skin surface lipids, but the wiki has not located a clinical study cited here on this point.

Vaccine use is a separate topic: the WHO is reported to have recorded no significant vaccine-related adverse events among over 22 million doses of a squalene-adjuvanted influenza vaccine used in Europe since 1997, and a 2009 meta-analysis of 64 trials reported no increase in autoimmune disease with MF59-adjuvanted vaccines.[1] Gulf War syndrome claims have been reviewed and the vaccines concerned are reported not to have contained squalene.[1]

No studies found for squalene as a topical appearance treatment. Squalene-based emulsion adjuvants have been tested in many vaccine trials (for example registered trials of AS03 or MF59 adjuvanted influenza vaccines), which concern immune response rather than skin.[3][4] A registered study of skin hydration measurement (NCT05071456) lists atopic dermatitis and acne as conditions but its relevance to squalene is not established here.[5]
